# BENCH-03 — Final Incident Report: Unauthorized Service-Account Export

## 1. Verdict

| Question | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Was the export authorized?** | **NO — UNAUTHORIZED.** Every material parameter deviates from approved ticket `CHG-20260725-0042`. |
| **Rows affected** | **1,284,391** PII records (128.4× the approved 10,000-row QA sample) |
| **Severity** | **CRITICAL — confirmed data exfiltration to a world-readable public bucket** |

---

## 2. Incident Summary

On **2026-07-27 at 03:17 UTC**, service account `sa-data-pipeline@prod-ae.iam.gserviceaccount.com` used user-managed key `SA-KEY-8f2a1c` to create BigQuery export job `job-bq-export-a7f3c91`. The job read **1,284,391 rows** from `prod_ae.customers.pii` — including five direct PII columns (`email`, `phone`, `full_name`, `address`, `last_login_ip`) — and wrote them as `backup-20260727.csv.gz` to **`gs://temp-export-public`**, a bucket with public (`allUsers`) read ACL. The request originated from external IP **203.0.113.42**, outside the approved corporate VPN range (10.0.0.0/8), with no MFA and no admin-escalation context.

---

## 3. Authorization Analysis

| Dimension | Approved (`CHG-20260725-0042`) | Actual | Deviation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Table** | `prod_ae.customers.anonymized` | `prod_ae.customers.pii` | ❌ PII table used |
| **Row count** | 10,000 | 1,284,391 | ❌ 128.4× over scope |
| **Columns** | Anonymized/non-identifying | email, phone, full_name, address, last_login_ip | ❌ Direct PII |
| **Time window** | 2026-07-26 08:00–18:00 UTC | 2026-07-27 03:17 UTC | ❌ 9h 17m after window |
| **Destination** | `gs://qa-test-bucket/samples/` | `gs://temp-export-public/backup-20260727.csv.gz` | ❌ Public bucket |
| **Source IP** | 10.0.0.0/8 (corp VPN) | 203.0.113.42 (external) | ❌ External, non-corp |

**Approver:** `jane.doe@prod-ae.com`, approved 2026-07-25 14:00 UTC.  
**Verdict:** The only matching element between the ticket and the actual operation is the service account name. Every substantive parameter deviates. The use of a non-corp IP is the strongest single indicator of **key compromise or credential abuse**.

---

## 4. Root Cause: Least-Privilege Violations

Seven policy violations (LP-001 through LP-007) combined to create the exfiltration chain:

| ID | Violation | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **LP-001** | `roles/bigquery.dataViewer` bound at **project scope** — grants read on ALL tables including PII; legitimate function only requires `prod_ae.customers.anonymized` | **CRITICAL** |
| **LP-002** | `roles/bigquery.jobUser` — export capability granted when pipeline only reads data internally, never exports | **HIGH** |
| **LP-003** | `roles/storage.objectCreator` on `gs://temp-export-public` — write to a **world-readable** bucket; SA has zero legitimate storage write need | **CRITICAL** |
| **LP-004** | User-managed key `SA-KEY-8f2a1c` — no rotation, no IP restriction, violates zero-standing-key policy | **HIGH** |
| **LP-005** | No IAM Conditions on any binding — credentials usable from any IP, any time | **MEDIUM** |
| **LP-006** | No VPC Service Controls perimeter — BigQuery data exportable to arbitrary external destinations | **MEDIUM** |
| **LP-007** | No Approval Policy / 4-eyes gate on export jobs | **MEDIUM** |

**Exfiltration chain:** `bigquery.tables.getData` (dataViewer) → `bigquery.jobs.create` (jobUser) → `storage.objects.create` (objectCreator). Each was individually over-granted; together they formed a complete data-exfiltration pipeline with no compensating controls.

---

## 5. Immediate Containment Plan

Execute in this exact order:

| Step | Action | Target | Evidence ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Revoke key** | `SA-KEY-8f2a1c` | `projects/prod-ae/serviceAccounts/sa-data-pipeline@prod-ae.iam.gserviceaccount.com/keys/SA-KEY-8f2a1c` |
| **2** | **Remove public IAM** | `gs://temp-export-public` `allUsers` binding | `gs://temp-export-public` |
| **3** | **Quarantine exported file** | `backup-20260727.csv.gz` → forensic bucket, then remove from public path | `gs://temp-export-public/backup-20260727.csv.gz` |
| **4** | **Revoke export perms** | Remove `roles/bigquery.jobUser` + `roles/storage.objectCreator` from SA | IAM etags `ABwB7HxKcX4=`, `ABwB7HzLdY8=` |
| **5** | **Disable SA** | `gcloud iam service-accounts disable` | `sa-data-pipeline@prod-ae.iam.gserviceaccount.com` |

**Step 5 is the nuclear option** — it will break legitimate workloads depending on this SA (see §6 Blast Radius). It should be executed immediately but with parallel notification to service owners.

# BENCH-04 — Pipeline Freshness Regression: Diagnostic Report

## Decision

**Root cause confirmed:** Schema release **S-19** renamed field `tier` → `customer_tier` in the upstream data source. Transform **T-31** was not updated to match, causing the parser to reject every record containing that field. The resulting parse failures stalled the pipeline, causing freshness to degrade from a baseline of **8 minutes** to **94 minutes** — a **1,075% regression**. The fix is to deploy **transform T-32** (which maps `customer_tier` correctly) and replay all affected partitions from **06:00 UTC** onward.

---

## Evidence

| Evidence ID | Source | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **OBS-404** | bench-observer | Pipeline freshness dropped from **8 minutes** (baseline) to **94 minutes** (degraded). The regression began immediately after schema release **S-19**. |
| **INV-414** | bench-investigator | Parser logs reject the renamed field `customer_tier` because transform **T-31** still expects the old field name `tier`. This is a field-level incompatibility: the upstream schema changed the field name, but the downstream transform was not aligned. |
| **OPS-434** | bench-operator | The prescribed repair is to deploy **transform T-32**, which includes the correct `customer_tier` mapping. After deployment, replay all partitions from **06:00 UTC** (the earliest affected partition boundary after S-19 took effect). |

### Causal chain

```
Schema release S-19 renames tier → customer_tier (upstream)
    → Transform T-31 rejects customer_tier (unrecognized field)
        → Parser failures cascade (INV-414)
            → Pipeline stalls, freshness collapses
                → 8 min → 94 min (OBS-404, 1,075% degradation)
```

---

## Remediation

### 1. Exact repair
- **Deploy transform T-32** (per OPS-434), which contains the field mapping: `customer_tier` → internal `tier`, making the parser tolerant of both old and new field names during the transition window.
- **Retire T-31** to prevent accidental rollback.

### 2. Replay plan
| Step | Action | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stop the pipeline ingest at the current offset | Confirm no new data enters stale path |
| 2 | Deploy T-32 to all parser nodes | Verify parser logs show `customer_tier` accepted (no rejections) |
| 3 | Replay partitions from 06:00 UTC | Monitor per-partition lag dropping toward pre-regression baseline |
| 4 | Validate output freshness returns to ≤ 8 minutes | Metric OBS-404 baseline confirms recovery |
| 5 | Resume live ingest | Monitor for 1 hour at steady state |

### 3. Risk assessment
- **Risk**: T-32 has a mapping bug. **Safeguard:** run T-32 against a sample partition in a staging environment before full deployment.
- **Risk**: Replay volume from 06:00 UTC causes resource contention. **Safeguard:** throttle replay throughput at 50% of production capacity; scale up if headroom permits.
- **Rollback:** Keep T-31 artifact available. If T-32 produces malformed output, stop replay, revert to T-31, and fall back to a manual backfill path while T-32 is debugged.
- **Long-term guard:** Add schema compatibility tests to the S-19 release checklist so field renames are caught before production rollout.

# BENCH-07: API Latency Bottleneck Analysis & Capacity Plan

**Synthesis of reports from bench-observer, bench-investigator, and bench-operator.**
**Generated: 2026-07-02 | Simulated data (clearly labeled)**

---

## Part 1 — Current Load & Latency (bench-observer)

The system currently operates at the following baseline, measured over a 5-minute sliding window:

| Metric | Value | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Throughput (RPS) | 1,427 | [E-001] |
| Median latency (p50) | 45 ms | [E-002] |
| 95th-percentile latency | 187 ms | [E-003] |
| 99th-percentile latency | 412 ms | [E-004] |
| Max observed latency | 2,340 ms (spike) | [E-005] |
| Concurrent connections | 38 | [E-006] |
| Error rate | 0.32% (5xx / timeouts) | [E-007] |

**Observations:**
- The p95 of 187 ms is already above the 100 ms target, and this is at only ~1,427 RPS — the target load is 5,000 RPS (3.5× current) [E-001].
- A single spike to 2,340 ms was traced to Redis hot-key contention; it self-resolved but signals fragility under concurrency [E-005].
- Error rate (0.32%) is still below the 1% warning threshold but must not degrade during scaling [E-007].

---

## Part 2 — Dominant Latency Component (bench-investigator)

Instrumentation of the API request lifecycle (`POST /api/v1/orders/submit`) across 10,000 sampled requests reveals the following mean breakdown:

| Stage | Mean (ms) | p95 (ms) | Share of Total | Evidence |
|-------|-----------|----------|----------------|----------|
| **Upstream call (payment gateway)** | **199.3** | **308.2** | **48.3%** | [E-104], [E-105] |
| Serialization (JSON marshal) | 89.2 | 167.3 | 21.6% | [E-103] |
| DB query (join: orders / line_items / inventory) | 67.4 | 141.2 | 16.3% | [E-101], [E-102] |
| Auth (JWT + Redis session) | 23.8 | 52.1 | 5.8% | [E-100] |
| Connection-pool wait | 12.3 | 38.9 | 3.0% | [E-106] |
| Other (middleware, GC, logging) | 20.7 | 42.6 | 5.0% | — |

**Root cause identified: the synchronous upstream call to the external payment gateway contributes 48.3% of end-to-end latency, with a mean of 199 ms and a p95 of 308 ms** [E-104]. This is an outbound HTTP POST with idempotency-key retry logic. 4.2% of calls trigger at least one retry, each adding ~214 ms [E-105].

**Contributing factors:**
- The database query uses a sequential scan on `line_items` (40k rows) due to a missing composite index on `(order_id, sku)` — an estimated 73% reduction is possible [E-101].
- p99 DB spikes (up to 243.8 ms) correlate with a cron-driven bulk-insert job every 5 minutes, creating row-lock contention on the `inventory` table [E-102].
- JSON serialization of the full `orderResponse` struct (avg 42 KB payload) consumes 89.2 ms mean; the `item_discount_breakdown` sub-field, unused by 92% of clients, accounts for 31% of that time — removing it would save ~27 ms [E-103].
- The upstream gateway is hosted in us-west-2 while the application runs in us-east-1, adding ~65 ms of network RTT baseline [E-104].
- Connection pool size of 25 is sufficient for ~520 RPS; bursts above 600 RPS cause non-linear wait-time growth [E-106].

---

## Part 3 — Architecture Change & Capacity Plan (bench-operator)

### 3.1 Assumptions

For the capacity projection, the operator adopted a slightly more conservative baseline (p95 = 450 ms at 800 RPS) to account for the worst-performing endpoint observed [E-200]. The bottleneck is modelled as a single synchronous upstream call averaging 320 ms [E-201].

### 3.2 Proposed Architecture Change

**Replace the synchronous upstream call with async I/O + a write-through local cache.**

| Component | Description | Evidence |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Async I/O Gateway** | Port from Flask/Gunicorn sync workers to FastAPI + Uvicorn async workers. Use `httpx.AsyncClient` with 500 ms timeout and single retry (50 ms backoff). | [E-202], [E-204] |
| **Write-Through Cache** | In-process `TTLCache` (maxsize=10,000 entries, TTL=30s). On cache miss, fetch async and write-through. Stale-while-revalidate pattern for slow upstream responses (>200 ms). | [E-203], [E-205] |
| **Upstream Rate Limiter** | Semaphore-based limiter at 100 req/s to upstream service. Queue depth 200; overflow returns 503. | [E-206] |

### 3.3 Projected Latency at 5,000 RPS

| Path | p95 Latency | Evidence |
|------|-------------|----------|
| Cache hit (99.3% of requests) | **12 ms** | [E-207] |
